/-!
# Hilbert's tenth problem for number fields

Hilbert's tenth problem asks for an algorithm which decides, for any given polynomial equation
with integer coefficients in any number of unknowns, whether it has a solution in the integers.
By the MRDP theorem (Davis, Putnam, Robinson, Matiyasevich, 1970) no such algorithm exists.

The same question can be asked for any countable ring $R$: *Hilbert's tenth problem for $R$*
asks for an algorithm which decides, for any polynomial equation with coefficients in $R$,
whether it has a solution in $R$. Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems asks: *for which number
fields does Hilbert's tenth problem hold?* Following the Wikipedia article, this is read as the
question for the rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ of number fields $K$. Undecidability was known
for many classes of number fields (Denef–Lipshitz, Shapiro–Shlapentokh, Pheidas, Videla, ...).
Koymans–Pagano (2024) and Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman (2025) have announced proofs that
Hilbert's tenth problem is undecidable for the ring of integers of *every* number field.
The problem for equations over the field $\mathbb{Q}$ itself remains open.

To speak about algorithms, a polynomial equation `P = 0` over a ring `R` is given by a *code*:
a finite list of terms `(c, m)`, where `c` codes a coefficient of `R` (decoded by a fixed map
`f`) and `m : List (ℕ × ℕ)` lists pairs `(i, k)` standing for the factors `X i ^ k` of a
monomial in the unknowns `X 0, X 1, …`. Every polynomial over `R` has such a code
(`PolyCode.toMvPolynomial_surjective`). The existence of an algorithm is rendered by
`ComputablePred` on the codes. For `R = 𝓞 K` the coefficients are coded by their coordinates
with respect to a `ℤ`-basis of `𝓞 K`; for `R = ℚ` they are rational numbers.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Hilbert's tenth problem*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [P. Koymans, C. Pagano, *Hilbert's tenth problem via additive combinatorics*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01768)
- [L. Alpöge, M. Bhargava, W. Ho, A. Shnidman, *Rank stability in quadratic extensions and
  Hilbert's tenth problem for the ring of integers of a number field*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18774)
-/

noncomputable def PolyCode.toMvPolynomial (f : α → R) (p : PolyCode α) : MvPolynomial ℕ R :=
  (p.map fun t => C (f t.1) * (t.2.map fun ik => X ik.1 ^ ik.2).prod).sum

The polynomial `∑ (c, m) ∈ p, f c * ∏ (i, k) ∈ m, X i ^ k` coded by `p`, where `f` decodes
the coefficients.

justification.closest_existing_considered: MvPolynomial.map (needs a RingHom; the basis-coordinate decoding is only ℤ-linear), MvPolynomial.rename.
justification.name: HilbertsTenthProblem.PolyCode.toMvPolynomial
justification.why_needed: Decodes a code to an element of MvPolynomial ℕ R given a coefficient decoding f : α → R (id for ℚ, ℤ; integral-basis coordinates for 𝓞 K). Proved surjective when f is (API lemma toMvPolynomial_surjective), so codes cover every polynomial equation.

blocks.name: PolyCode.toMvPolynomial
blocks.text:
/--
The polynomial `∑ (c, m) ∈ p, f c * ∏ (i, k) ∈ m, X i ^ k` coded by `p`, where `f` decodes

-/
noncomputable def PolyCode.toMvPolynomial (f : α → R) (p : PolyCode α) : MvPolynomial ℕ R :=

blocks.code:
def PolyCode.HasSolution (f : α → R) (p : PolyCode α) : Prop :=
  ∃ x : ℕ → R, eval x (p.toMvPolynomial f) = 0
blocks.docstring:
The polynomial equation coded by `p` (with coefficients decoded by `f : α → R`) has a solution
in `R`. Only the finitely many unknowns occurring in `p` matter.

justification.closest_existing_considered: No existing 'Diophantine equation has a solution' predicate in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib.
justification.name: HilbertsTenthProblem.PolyCode.HasSolution
justification.why_needed: The decision predicate: ∃ x : ℕ → R, eval x (p.toMvPolynomial f) = 0. Variables are indexed by ℕ; each code mentions finitely many so this is equivalent to solvability in finitely many unknowns.

blocks.code:
@[category API, AMS 3 12]
theorem PolyCode.toMvPolynomial_surjective {f : α → R} (hf : Function.Surjective f) :
    Function.Surjective (PolyCode.toMvPolynomial f) := by
  intro P
  induction P using MvPolynomial.induction_on with
  | C a =>
    obtain ⟨c, rfl⟩ := hf a
    exact ⟨[(c, [])], by simp [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial]⟩
  | add P Q hP hQ =>
    obtain ⟨p, rfl⟩ := hP
    obtain ⟨q, rfl⟩ := hQ
    exact ⟨p ++ q, by simp [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial]⟩
  | mul_X P i hP =>
    obtain ⟨p, rfl⟩ := hP
    refine ⟨p.map fun t => (t.1, t.2 ++ [(i, 1)]), ?_⟩
    simp only [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial, List.map_map, Function.comp_def, List.map_append,
      List.prod_append, List.map_cons, List.map_nil, List.prod_cons, List.prod_nil, pow_one,
      mul_one, ← mul_assoc]
    rw [List.sum_map_mul_right]
blocks.docstring: Every polynomial over `R` is coded by some `p : PolyCode α` when `f : α → R` is surjective.

@[category research open, AMS 3 11]
theorem hilberts_tenth_problem (K : Type*) [Field K] [NumberField K] {d : ℕ}
    (b : Module.Basis (Fin d) ℤ (𝓞 K)) :
    ¬ ComputablePred fun p : PolyCode (Fin d → ℤ) => p.HasSolution b.equivFun.symm := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
**Hilbert's tenth problem for the ring of integers of a number field.**

Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems asks: *for which number fields does Hilbert's tenth
problem hold?* Read as the classical question for rings of integers, the expected answer is
"for every number field": for every number field $K$ there is no algorithm which decides, for
any given polynomial equation with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_K$ in any number of unknowns,
whether it has a solution in $\mathcal{O}_K$.

Elements of `𝓞 K` are coded by their coordinate vectors `Fin d → ℤ` with respect to a `ℤ`-basis
`b` of `𝓞 K` (decoded by `b.equivFun.symm`), and polynomial equations by `PolyCode (Fin d → ℤ)`.
Any two such bases differ by an integer matrix, so decidability does not depend on `b`.

Proofs of this statement have been announced by Koymans–Pagano (2024) and by
Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman (2025).

blocks.docstring:
**Hilbert's tenth problem over the rationals.**

Does there exist an algorithm which decides, for any given polynomial equation with rational
coefficients in any number of unknowns, whether it has a solution in rational numbers?
Here `answer(True)` means that such an algorithm exists. Despite much interest, this problem
remains open.

claims.decomposer_note: Read as the classical classification question for rings of integers O_K (the reading matching the article's Denef–Lipshitz / Shapiro–Shlapentokh / Pheidas results indexed by properties of K); the article and both cited arXiv papers (Koymans–Pagano 2412.01768, Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman 2501.18774) assert the candidate answer 'all number fields', so the Prop is: for every number field K there is no algorithm deciding whether a polynomial equation with coefficients in O_K has a solution in O_K (equivalently ℤ is Diophantine over O_K); 'algorithm' must be rendered via computability of a predicate on encodings of polynomials, and the article calls the proofs 'claimed', so category is debatable (research solved vs open).
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same Prop (for every number field K, the solvability predicate on codes of polynomial equations over 𝓞 K is not a ComputablePred) and differ only in encoding details. The final file uses c02's skeleton (PolyCode = List (coeff × List (ℕ × ℕ)), toMvPolynomial into MvPolynomial ℕ R, HasSolution := ∃ x : ℕ → R, eval x P = 0, surjectivity API lemma, exists_basis, test examples) with c01's naming and the decoding `b.equivFun.symm` used by c04/c06/c07 (equal to c01/c02's `fun c => ∑ i, c i • b i`, but visibly bijective). Quantifying over an arbitrary ℤ-basis b : Basis (Fin d) ℤ (𝓞 K) is faithful: every number field has such a basis (proved as exists_basis), and any two bases are related by a computable change of coordinates, so each instance is exactly 'H10 for 𝓞 K is undecidable'. ℕ-indexed unknowns are equivalent to finitely many unknowns since each code mentions finitely many variables. Rejected alternatives: c03 (odd ∃ d, Nonempty (≃+) ∧ ∀ decode structure, universe-restricted K : Type, minimal docstring), c05 (quantifies over arbitrary Primcodable (𝓞 K) with computable +,*; correct by a presentation-independence argument but harder to audit), c08 (fixes Module.finBasis; fine but less transparent), c04 (extra Mathlib imports, binders inside the statement), c06 (adds non-slot research theorems). Category kept `research open` per the supplied status; docstring records the announced proofs.

context:
Hilbert's tenth problem is the tenth on the list of mathematical problems that the German mathematician David Hilbert posed in 1900.  It is the challenge to provide a general algorithm that, for any given Diophantine equation (a polynomial equation with integer coefficients and a finite number of unknowns), can decide whether the equation has a solution with all unknowns taking integer values.
For example, the Diophantine equation $3x^{2}-2xy-y^{2}z-7=0$ has an integer solution: $x=1,\ y=2,\ z=-2$. By contrast, the Diophantine equation $x^{2}+y^{2}+1=0$ has no such solution.
The solution to Hilbert's tenth problem shows that such a general algorithm cannot exist. This is the result of combined work of Martin Davis, Yuri Matiyasevich, Hilary Putnam, and Julia Robinson spanning 21 years, with Matiyasevich completing the theorem in 1970. The theorem is now known as Matiyasevich's theorem or the MRDP theorem (an initialism for the surnames of the four principal contributors to its solution).
When all coefficients and variables are restricted to be positive integers, the related problem of polynomial identity testing is a decidable (exponentiation-free) variation of Tarski's high school algebra problem, sometimes denoted ${\overline {HSI}}.$ == Background ==

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Hilbert's tenth problem for number fields

Hilbert's tenth problem asks for an algorithm which decides, for any given polynomial equation
with integer coefficients in any number of unknowns, whether it has a solution in the integers.
By the MRDP theorem (Davis, Putnam, Robinson, Matiyasevich, 1970) no such algorithm exists.

The same question can be asked for any countable ring $R$: *Hilbert's tenth problem for $R$*
asks for an algorithm which decides, for any polynomial equation with coefficients in $R$,
whether it has a solution in $R$. Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems asks: *for which number
fields does Hilbert's tenth problem hold?* Following the Wikipedia article, this is read as the
question for the rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ of number fields $K$. Undecidability was known
for many classes of number fields (Denef–Lipshitz, Shapiro–Shlapentokh, Pheidas, Videla, ...).
Koymans–Pagano (2024) and Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman (2025) have announced proofs that
Hilbert's tenth problem is undecidable for the ring of integers of *every* number field.
The problem for equations over the field $\mathbb{Q}$ itself remains open.

To speak about algorithms, a polynomial equation `P = 0` over a ring `R` is given by a *code*:
a finite list of terms `(c, m)`, where `c` codes a coefficient of `R` (decoded by a fixed map
`f`) and `m : List (ℕ × ℕ)` lists pairs `(i, k)` standing for the factors `X i ^ k` of a
monomial in the unknowns `X 0, X 1, …`. Every polynomial over `R` has such a code
(`PolyCode.toMvPolynomial_surjective`). The existence of an algorithm is rendered by
`ComputablePred` on the codes. For `R = 𝓞 K` the coefficients are coded by their coordinates
with respect to a `ℤ`-basis of `𝓞 K`; for `R = ℚ` they are rational numbers.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Hilbert's tenth problem*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [P. Koymans, C. Pagano, *Hilbert's tenth problem via additive combinatorics*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01768)
- [L. Alpöge, M. Bhargava, W. Ho, A. Shnidman, *Rank stability in quadratic extensions and
  Hilbert's tenth problem for the ring of integers of a number field*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18774)
-/

namespace HilbertsTenthProblem

open MvPolynomial NumberField

variable {α R : Type*} [CommSemiring R]

/--
A code for a polynomial equation `P = 0` in the unknowns `X 0, X 1, …`, with coefficients coded
by elements of `α`. A code is a finite list of terms `(c, m)`: `c : α` codes the coefficient of
the term and `m` lists pairs `(i, k)` standing for the factors `X i ^ k` of its monomial.
-/
abbrev PolyCode (α : Type*) := List (α × List (ℕ × ℕ))

/--
The polynomial `∑ (c, m) ∈ p, f c * ∏ (i, k) ∈ m, X i ^ k` coded by `p`, where `f` decodes
the coefficients.
-/
noncomputable def PolyCode.toMvPolynomial (f : α → R) (p : PolyCode α) : MvPolynomial ℕ R :=
  (p.map fun t => C (f t.1) * (t.2.map fun ik => X ik.1 ^ ik.2).prod).sum

/--
The polynomial equation coded by `p` (with coefficients decoded by `f : α → R`) has a solution
in `R`. Only the finitely many unknowns occurring in `p` matter.
-/
def PolyCode.HasSolution (f : α → R) (p : PolyCode α) : Prop :=
  ∃ x : ℕ → R, eval x (p.toMvPolynomial f) = 0

/-- Every polynomial over `R` is coded by some `p : PolyCode α` when `f : α → R` is surjective. -/
@[category API, AMS 3 12]
theorem PolyCode.toMvPolynomial_surjective {f : α → R} (hf : Function.Surjective f) :
    Function.Surjective (PolyCode.toMvPolynomial f) := by
  intro P
  induction P using MvPolynomial.induction_on with
  | C a =>
    obtain ⟨c, rfl⟩ := hf a
    exact ⟨[(c, [])], by simp [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial]⟩
  | add P Q hP hQ =>
    obtain ⟨p, rfl⟩ := hP
    obtain ⟨q, rfl⟩ := hQ
    exact ⟨p ++ q, by simp [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial]⟩
  | mul_X P i hP =>
    obtain ⟨p, rfl⟩ := hP
    refine ⟨p.map fun t => (t.1, t.2 ++ [(i, 1)]), ?_⟩
    simp only [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial, List.map_map, Function.comp_def, List.map_append,
      List.prod_append, List.map_cons, List.map_nil, List.prod_cons, List.prod_nil, pow_one,
      mul_one, ← mul_assoc]
    rw [List.sum_map_mul_right]

/-- The code of the equation $x^2 + y^2 + 1 = 0$ over `ℤ`. -/
@[category test, AMS 3 11]
theorem PolyCode.toMvPolynomial_example :
    PolyCode.toMvPolynomial (id : ℤ → ℤ) [(1, [(0, 2)]), (1, [(1, 2)]), (1, [])] =
      X 0 ^ 2 + X 1 ^ 2 + 1 := by
  simp [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial, add_assoc]

/-- The equation $x^2 + y^2 + 1 = 0$ has no integer solution. -/
@[category test, AMS 3 11]
theorem PolyCode.not_hasSolution_example :
    ¬ PolyCode.HasSolution (id : ℤ → ℤ) [(1, [(0, 2)]), (1, [(1, 2)]), (1, [])] := by
  rintro ⟨x, hx⟩
  simp [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial] at hx
  nlinarith [sq_nonneg (x 0), sq_nonneg (x 1)]

/-- The equation $3x^2 - 2xy - y^2z - 7 = 0$ has the integer solution $x = 1$, $y = 2$,
$z = -2$. -/
@[category test, AMS 3 11]
theorem PolyCode.hasSolution_example :
    PolyCode.HasSolution (id : ℤ → ℤ)
      [(3, [(0, 2)]), (-2, [(0, 1), (1, 1)]), (-1, [(1, 2), (2, 1)]), (-7, [])] := by
  refine ⟨fun n => match n with | 0 => 1 | 1 => 2 | _ => -2, ?_⟩
  simp [PolyCode.toMvPolynomial]

/--
The ring of integers of a number field has a `ℤ`-basis indexed by `Fin d` for some `d`, so the
hypothesis of `hilberts_tenth_problem` can be satisfied for every number field.
-/
@[category API, AMS 11]
theorem exists_basis (K : Type*) [Field K] [NumberField K] :
    ∃ d : ℕ, Nonempty (Module.Basis (Fin d) ℤ (𝓞 K)) :=
  ⟨_, ⟨Module.finBasis ℤ (𝓞 K)⟩⟩

/--
**Hilbert's tenth problem for the ring of integers of a number field.**

Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems asks: *for which number fields does Hilbert's tenth
problem hold?* Read as the classical question for rings of integers, the expected answer is
"for every number field": for every number field $K$ there is no algorithm which decides, for
any given polynomial equation with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_K$ in any number of unknowns,
whether it has a solution in $\mathcal{O}_K$.

Elements of `𝓞 K` are coded by their coordinate vectors `Fin d → ℤ` with respect to a `ℤ`-basis
`b` of `𝓞 K` (decoded by `b.equivFun.symm`), and polynomial equations by `PolyCode (Fin d → ℤ)`.
Any two such bases differ by an integer matrix, so decidability does not depend on `b`.

Proofs of this statement have been announced by Koymans–Pagano (2024) and by
Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman (2025).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 11]
theorem hilberts_tenth_problem (K : Type*) [Field K] [NumberField K] {d : ℕ}
    (b : Module.Basis (Fin d) ℤ (𝓞 K)) :
    ¬ ComputablePred fun p : PolyCode (Fin d → ℤ) => p.HasSolution b.equivFun.symm := by
  sorry

/--
**Hilbert's tenth problem over the rationals.**

Does there exist an algorithm which decides, for any given polynomial equation with rational
coefficients in any number of unknowns, whether it has a solution in rational numbers?
Here `answer(True)` means that such an algorithm exists. Despite much interest, this problem
remains open.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 11]
theorem hilberts_tenth_problem.variants.rationals :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ComputablePred fun p : PolyCode ℚ => p.HasSolution id := by
  sorry

end HilbertsTenthProblem

items: Reading of the list entry: following the decomposition table and the article, 'Hilbert's tenth problem for a number field K' means the decision problem for polynomial equations with coefficients in 𝓞 K and solutions in 𝓞 K, and the candidate answer 'all number fields' (undecidable for every K) is what is stated as the Prop.

Category: both slots are tagged `research open` to match the given status 'open'. Note that Koymans–Pagano (arXiv:2412.01768) and Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman (arXiv:2501.18774) have announced proofs of the main slot; the Wikipedia article calls them 'claimed' and the list still records the problem as open. A reviewer may prefer `research solved` for the main slot.

'Algorithm' is rendered by Mathlib's `ComputablePred` on a Primcodable type of codes for polynomial equations. A code is `List (R × List (ℕ × ℕ))`: a list of terms (coefficient code, list of (variable index, exponent) pairs). The map `toMvPolynomial f` sends a code to the polynomial ∑ f c * ∏ X i ^ k in `MvPolynomial ℕ S`; it is proven surjective when `f` is surjective (`toMvPolynomial_surjective`), so every polynomial equation over S is coded. Since all reasonable codings of polynomials are computably inter-translatable, the choice of this particular coding does not affect the decidability claim.

Unknowns are indexed by ℕ and solutions are `x : ℕ → S`; each coded polynomial involves only finitely many variables, so this is equivalent to 'finitely many unknowns' in the usual sense (the decomposition note mentions Fin n; ℕ-indexing avoids a spurious bound parameter).

Coefficients in 𝓞 K are coded by integer coordinate vectors `Fin n → ℤ` with respect to a ℤ-basis `b` of 𝓞 K (decoded by `fun c => ∑ i, c i • b i`). The theorem quantifies over all n and all such bases; the truth value is independent of the basis (change of basis is a computable bijection on codes), and for n ≠ [K:ℚ] the hypothesis is unsatisfiable (harmlessly vacuous). Non-vacuity is witnessed by the proven API lemma `exists_basis` (via `Module.finBasis`). An alternative would be to quantify over arbitrary computable presentations of 𝓞 K (a Primcodable type with computable ring operations ring-isomorphic to 𝓞 K); the basis presentation was chosen as the concrete standard one.

For the rationals slot, coefficients are literal elements of ℚ (Mathlib provides `Primcodable ℚ`), and the equivalence direction is: answer(True) means an algorithm exists, answer(False) means none exists. The widespread expectation of undecidability is not asserted, as the sources do not state it as a conjecture.

Extra declarations beyond the two slots are only API/test statements for the bespoke definitions (surjectivity of the coding, the two example equations from the Wikipedia article, existence of a basis); no additional research-level statement (e.g. MRDP for ℤ) was added since it is not in the decomposition table.

The literal classification question is not statable as a Prop, so the 'Dropped' entry with the same text span was treated as a bookkeeping artifact (as all candidates did). Two independent proofs of the main slot have been announced (Koymans–Pagano arXiv:2412.01768, Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman arXiv:2501.18774) and the article calls them 'claimed'; a maintainer may prefer `research solved` (the repo's Paper/BranchingVAS.lean tags a recently announced result as solved).
